How Tide Pools Survive the Winter

Every winter the rocky shore along the northern coast loses most of its daylight, and the tide pools that seemed so lively in August turn grey and quiet. Marine biologists have long wondered how the small creatures living in them cope with the cold, the storms and the long nights.

Anemones close up shop

Sea anemones pull their tentacles inward and cover themselves with a thin layer of mucus. This keeps them from drying out when the tide is low and the wind is strong, and it also protects them from the sand that winter waves throw against the rocks.

Researchers measured the metabolism of anemones in three pools over two seasons and found that it drops by almost half between November and February, which lets the animals live on the energy they stored during the summer months.

Crabs move to deeper water

Shore crabs do not stay in the pools at all. They walk down to deeper water below the low tide line, where the temperature changes much more slowly, and they come back only when the days grow longer again in early spring.
